opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it is just the pace of the field. In AI, things move so fast that if you hedge everything and wrap your opinion in layers of politeness and qualification, the moment has already passed by the time people figure out what you meant. You don't have the luxury of being vague. If you think a direction is wrong, or a result isn't going to scale, you should say so clearly, because people are making decisions about where to spend compute, time, and careers based on these judgments.

The other part is that the culture rewards being concretely wrong more than being vaguely right. When I was doing physics, especially more theoretical work, there was room to be careful and abstract. A lot of discussion stayed at the level of "this is interesting" or "this might be related." In AI, especially in a frontier lab, you very quickly get feedback from experiments. So the useful thing is to make a sharp claim, like "I think this will work, and here's why," and then let reality check you. If you're wrong, fine, you update. But if you never commit to a view, you never learn anything.

There's also a personal side. Coming from a fairly traditional Chinese academic background, I was trained to be humble, not to stand out, and to defer to people more senior than me. Those aren't bad values. But in this environment I realized that if I didn't say what I actually thought, I wasn't really contributing. People around me were very direct, not in a rude way, just honest, and that made me feel it was not only okay but actually expected. Over time it became natural.

And honestly, it's more efficient and more respectful. Being direct means trusting the other person to handle disagreement and engage with the substance. I've come to see that as a form of respect rather than a lack of it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says experiments provide feedback and claims can be checked against reality, but does not connect objective performance standards to a lower risk of offending others when expressing internally coherent views.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes from a few places. The first is that the field moves so fast that there's simply no time to be vague. If I hedge everything, say "maybe this, maybe that," by the time the conversation is over, the landscape has already shifted. Being direct is almost a survival skill. You put your view out, it gets tested quickly, and if you're wrong, you find out fast and update. That feedback loop is actually a gift. In many other fields, you can hold a wrong opinion for ten years and nobody notices. In AI, you'll know in six months.

The second thing is that I've seen how much progress depends on people being willing to say something that sounds a bit naive or a bit contrarian. When we were doing things like ReAct or thinking about language agents, a lot of the ideas sounded almost too simple at first. If I had been careful about protecting my image, I probably wouldn't have pushed them. So I learned that the cost of sounding wrong is low, and the cost of staying quiet is high.

And honestly, there's a third part that's more personal. Working close to these systems changes how you think about your own thinking. You spend all day asking a model to state its reasoning clearly, to commit to an answer, to not waffle. At some point you realize you should hold yourself to the same standard. It would be a little hypocritical to demand clarity from the model and then be mushy myself.

I'd also say directness isn't the same as being certain. I'm often not certain. But I try to say exactly what I believe and roughly how confident I am, rather than hiding behind ambiguity. I think that's more respectful to the people I'm talking with, and it's more useful for the field. If everyone is polite and noncommittal, the conversation goes nowhere. If people say what they actually think, you can disagree productively, and that's where the interesting stuff happens.

r001.rationale: The response says AI’s fast feedback makes it easier to discover and correct wrong views, but it does not attribute lower risk of offending others to objective performance standards.

astra-6.text:
I think working in AI forces me to turn vague intuitions into explicit claims. It’s easy to say, “This approach seems promising.” But if you actually want to build something, you have to explain what you expect to happen, why, and what result would change your mind. That habit carries over into how I express my views.

And the field moves so quickly that you get used to being wrong. You can state a view clearly today and revise it tomorrow. Those things don’t have to conflict. In fact, being direct makes revision easier, because people can understand exactly what you believed and where they disagree.

So for me, being more direct doesn’t mean being more certain. It means making my current thinking clear enough that we can have a useful discussion about it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI requires explicit, testable claims and comfort with revising views, but does not mention objective performance standards or connect them to a lower risk of offending others.

sol-6.1.text:
I think working in AI pushes you to make your intuitions explicit. You can have a view that sounds reasonable, but once you try to turn it into an experiment, you have to say exactly what you mean. What do you expect to happen? What result would change your mind?

That’s gradually affected how I communicate, too. I’m more willing to say, “This is what I think, and this is why,” even if I’m uncertain. Being direct doesn’t have to mean being very confident. You can state your view clearly and still be ready to revise it. And once you put it clearly, other people can actually challenge it, which helps you learn faster.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments make intuitions explicit and views open to challenge, but it does not connect objective performance standards to a lower risk of offending others.
